title: Погром в баре  (Chaos at the Bar)

segments.t: At the Claude Monet bar, Kostya is horrified to find shattered glass everywhere and six bottles of elite cognac missing or broken while Ainura mops the floor. Listen to the whole exchange first, and then we will break it down line by line.
У тебя неудачное шоу в баре?
Забыли закрыть, и ночью кто-то забрался.
Now let's go back through their conversation line by line and unpack the Russian phrasing.
'Kostya, what happened here?' Max presses plainly on the spot, putting "zdes" ("here") alongside "sluchilos" ("happened") in a tight, everyday turn of phrase.
У тебя неудачное шоу в баре?
'Did you have a bad bartender show?' Max checks quietly in the room, linking "neudachnoye" ("unsuccessfully"), "shou" ("show"), and "bare" ("bar") in one brisk exchange.
'I will find out who was juggling here at night.' Kostya sustains a steady style straight away, building the phrase around "uznayu" ("to recognise") and "zdes" ("here") for a crisp, natural delivery.
'Ainura, could you clean up faster?' Kostya tests warmly as the talk turns, putting "mozhno" ("may, can") alongside "ubrat" ("to remove, to cut out") in a tight, everyday turn of phrase.
'Listen, Kostya, do not bother me.' Ainura displays a sharp tone straight away, putting "slushay" ("listen") alongside "meshay" ("bother") in a tight, everyday turn of phrase.
'Let me breathe in the expensive cognac a bit.' Ainura adopts an honest tack as they talk, putting "day" ("give") alongside "dorogim" ("expensive, dear") in a tight, everyday turn of phrase.
'They smashed three bottles last night.' Kostya offers a direct posture beside Ainura, weaving "butylki" ("bottle") together with "razbili" ("smashed, wrecked") just the way native speakers do.
'Maybe only two bottles?' Max wonders steadily from the start, anchoring the Russian line on "mozhet" ("can") and "byt" ("be") without extra filler.
'No, not two, three.' Kostya projects a brisk attitude without hesitation, building the phrase around "dve" ("two") and "tri" ("three") for a crisp, natural delivery.
Забыли закрыть, и ночью кто-то забрался.

'They forgot to lock up, and someone broke in at night.' Kostya maintains a grounded direction in the scene, weaving "zabyli" ("have you forgotten") together with "zakryt" ("to close, to shut") just the way native speakers do.
'Who could have done that?' Max inquires promptly to make the point, anchoring the Russian line on "mog" ("can, to be able") and "sdelat" ("to do") without extra filler.
'Well of course, not me.' Kostya presents a steady tone toward Max, linking "konechno" ("of course"), "nu" ("oh, come on"), and "ne" ("not") in one brisk exchange.
'And what are you doing here?' Ainura checks promptly without holding back, linking "tut" ("here"), "delayete" ("are doing"), and "vy" ("you") in one brisk exchange.
У тебя неудачное шоу в баре?
Забыли закрыть, и ночью кто-то забрался.
Max suddenly realizes why there were two extra bottles in Katya's apartment. Next, Chef Barinov walks in with a massive hangover of his own. Until next time!
